metaTitle: Best Mesh WiFi Systems for Homes
metaDescription: Six mesh WiFi systems compared on Wi-Fi generation, backhaul, ports and coverage claims, with picks for apartments, large homes and wired setups.
expertTake: The TP-Link Deco 7 Pro is our top pick for homes that can run Ethernet between nodes and want tri-band Wi-Fi 7, and the TP-Link Deco X55 is the value pick for a typical mid-size home on a gigabit plan. If your home is small enough for one good router to reach every room, skip mesh and buy a single router instead.
introParagraphs: A mesh Wi-Fi system replaces one router with several nodes that share one network name, so your phone roams without dropping calls. It fixes dead zones that a single router cannot reach through walls, floors and brick.

Mesh is not magic, though. Every wireless hop between nodes costs speed, and the speed labels on the box add every band together. This guide compares six systems on generation, backhaul, ports and ownership so you buy for your house, not for a number.

products.name: TP-Link Deco 7 Pro BE10000 tri-band Wi-Fi 7 mesh, 2.5G ports
products.description:
The Deco 7 Pro is a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 system in which one radio band can serve as a dedicated link between nodes. It lists 2.5 gigabit Ethernet ports and supports wired backhaul, which is the best way to keep full speed at distant nodes. The BE10000 label is the total of all bands combined, not what one device receives.

The tradeoff is cost and device support. At tier nine of eleven it is among the most expensive here, and Wi-Fi 7 only helps devices that also support it, which is still a minority. Compared with the Deco 7 dual-band model, which sits three tiers lower, the Pro adds a dedicated third band, so wireless backhaul loses less speed.

In ownership terms, the system is controlled from an app, and firmware updates arrive automatically. Plan to place the nodes about halfway between the main node and the dead zone, not inside it. Some security and parental features may depend on a subscription, so check which are free.
products.bestFor: Large homes with a wired backbone or a plan above one gigabit.
pros: Tri-band design reserves a band for node-to-node traffic
2.5G ports use plans and wired links above one gigabit
Wired backhaul keeps full speed at distant nodes
Wi-Fi 7 gives headroom as client devices catch up
cons: High price tier for homes that do not need the speed
Wi-Fi 7 benefits only appear with Wi-Fi 7 devices
Some advanced features may sit behind a subscription

products.name: NETGEAR Orbi 770 Wi-Fi 7 mesh, up to 8,000 sq ft, 3-pack
products.description:
NETGEAR's Orbi 770 is a Wi-Fi 7 system that lists coverage of up to 8,000 square feet from a three-pack and support for 100 devices. The nodes are larger than a typical mesh puck, a sign of the antenna and radio hardware inside. It is designed for big houses with many connected devices.

The compromise is cost and the nature of the claims. At tier ten of eleven it is nearly the most expensive here, and the 8,000 square foot figure is a best case in open space, not a promise through brick and metal. Compared with the Deco 7 Pro at tier nine, the Orbi lists higher coverage and speed, but both rely on Wi-Fi 7 devices to show their gains.

For ownership, keep nodes in open positions and avoid hiding them in cabinets. Firmware is delivered through the app, and some security extras require a subscription. A larger node footprint also means more space and power use, on the order of 10 to 20 watts per node.
products.bestFor: Big houses with many devices where coverage is the first concern.
pros: Largest listed coverage in the lineup, up to 8,000 sq ft
Wi-Fi 7 radios provide headroom for future devices
Listed support for 100 devices suits smart homes
Three-pack comes ready to cover a large floor plan
cons: Near the top of the price scale at tier ten of eleven
Coverage claims are best case in open space
Some security features may need a paid subscription

products.name: TP-Link Deco 7 BE5000 dual-band Wi-Fi 7 mesh, up to 6,600 sq ft
products.description:
The Deco 7 is a dual-band Wi-Fi 7 system with a listed 240 MHz channel capability and 2.5 gigabit Ethernet ports on each node. With only two bands, the wireless link between nodes shares airtime with client devices, so it is best used where nodes can be reached by Ethernet or are close together. It is a way to get Wi-Fi 7 features at a lower tier.

The tradeoff is backhaul. Next to the tri-band Deco 7 Pro, it has no dedicated link band, so a far node can slow down on wireless backhaul. At tier six of eleven it costs less than the Pro, but compared with the Deco X55 at tier three, the extra spend buys Wi-Fi 7 and 2.5G ports rather than extra coverage.

Setup takes minutes through the app. Place nodes about halfway to the dead zone, and wire them if possible. Expect firmware updates to arrive automatically, and check whether the features you want are free.
products.bestFor: Mid-size homes that want Wi-Fi 7 and 2.5G ports at a middle tier.
pros: Wi-Fi 7 and 2.5G ports at a middle price tier
Listed 240 MHz channel support gives device headroom
Wired nodes remove the dual-band backhaul penalty
Coverage up to 6,600 sq ft is listed for the three-pack
cons: Dual-band design shares airtime for wireless backhaul
Wi-Fi 7 gains appear only on Wi-Fi 7 client devices
Far nodes slow down without a wired link

products.name: TP-Link Deco XE75 AXE5400 tri-band Wi-Fi 6E, 3-pack
products.description:
The Deco XE75 is a Wi-Fi 6E system with tri-band radios, adding the 6 gigahertz band that is cleaner than the crowded 2.4 and 5 gigahertz bands. One band can handle the link between nodes, which keeps the other two free for devices. The listing claims coverage up to 7,200 square feet from a three-pack.

The compromise is that Wi-Fi 6E is a generation behind Wi-Fi 7, and its ports are the more common gigabit type, so it will not use a plan above one gigabit over Ethernet. At tier four of eleven, though, it is far cheaper than the Deco 7 Pro at tier nine, and a tri-band design is a real advantage over the dual-band Deco X55 in the same price neighbourhood.

Ownership is easy. Update through the app, place nodes about halfway to the weak area, and expect firmware support to continue for a few years. Check the 6 GHz benefit against your own devices, since many still use 5 GHz.
products.bestFor: Homes that want tri-band backhaul without paying Wi-Fi 7 prices.
pros: Tri-band layout keeps node links off the device bands
6 GHz band is less crowded than 2.4 and 5 GHz
Low price tier for a three-pack with tri-band radios
Coverage up to 7,200 sq ft is listed for the pack
cons: Wi-Fi 6E is a generation behind Wi-Fi 7
Gigabit ports cannot use a plan above one gigabit over wire
6 GHz needs 6E devices to make a difference

products.name: Amazon eero 6+ mesh Wi-Fi system, up to 4,500 sq ft
products.description:
Amazon's eero 6+ is a Wi-Fi 6 system aimed at gigabit plans, with coverage listed up to 4,500 square feet. It is built around a minimal app and a small, quiet node design that fits a living room shelf. The focus is on easy setup and steady everyday performance, not top speeds.

The tradeoff is range and extras. At 4,500 square feet, the claim is well below the Deco XE75 at 7,200 and the Orbi 770 at 8,000, and it supports plans only up to one gigabit. At tier five of eleven it costs more than the Deco X55 at tier three, so the premium pays for the app and ecosystem rather than hardware.

In ownership, the app is simple, firmware arrives automatically and the nodes are easy to move. Some security and parental features are tied to a subscription, so check what is free. For small and mid-size homes, it is a low-maintenance system.
products.bestFor: Smaller homes and renters who want a very simple app and setup.
pros: Simple app guides setup in minutes with little tuning
Compact nodes blend into a living room
Matches gigabit internet plans without extra complexity
Automatic firmware updates keep maintenance low
cons: Coverage claim is smaller than the TP-Link and Orbi packs
Limited to plans up to one gigabit
Some features may require a subscription

products.name: TP-Link Deco X55 AX3000 Wi-Fi 6 mesh, up to 6,500 sq ft, 3-pack
products.description:
The Deco X55 is a dual-band Wi-Fi 6 system sold as a three-pack, with listed coverage up to 6,500 square feet. It uses the AX3000 label, which is the sum of the two bands, so no single device will reach that figure. It replaces a router and extenders with nodes that share one network name.

The compromise is backhaul and generation. As a dual-band system, wireless links between nodes share airtime with devices, and Wi-Fi 6 lacks the extra channel width of Wi-Fi 7. At tier three of eleven it is far cheaper than the Deco 7 and Deco 7 Pro, so for a normal home on a gigabit plan, you pay little for a good result.

Ownership is simple. Set up in the app, place nodes about halfway between the main node and the weak room, and wire them if you can. Check that the ports are gigabit, which matches most plans.
products.bestFor: Typical mid-size homes on a gigabit plan that want the lowest tier.
pros: Three-pack with large listed coverage at a low price tier
Wi-Fi 6 is mature, stable and widely supported by devices
App setup is quick and does not need networking skills
Wired backhaul is possible to improve far nodes
cons: Dual-band design shares airtime for wireless backhaul
No 2.5G ports for plans above one gigabit
Wi-Fi 6 lacks the extra headroom of Wi-Fi 7

buyingCriteria.explanation: Backhaul is the link between nodes, and each wireless hop can cut speed. Tri-band systems like the Deco 7 Pro and Deco XE75 dedicate a band to it, while dual-band ones like the Deco X55 share it. Ethernet between nodes avoids the penalty, which is why 2.5G ports matter. Buyers often skip this and wonder why the far node is slow.

Wi-Fi 6 is mature, 6E adds the 6 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 adds wider channels and multi-link. The Deco 7 and Orbi 770 are Wi-Fi 7, the Deco XE75 is 6E, and the Deco X55 and eero 6+ are Wi-Fi 6. Your phones and laptops must support the same standard to benefit. Most homes see little gain from Wi-Fi 7 yet.

Square footage claims are best case, in open space. The Orbi 770 lists 8,000 sq ft and the eero 6+ lists 4,500, but walls, brick and metal reduce both. Count floors and thick walls, not only area. A three-pack suits a large home, and a small home may need only two nodes.

Internet plans above one gigabit need a 2.5G WAN port to use them. The Deco 7 and Deco 7 Pro list 2.5G ports, while the Deco X55 and eero 6+ do not. Ethernet ports on nodes also vary in number, which matters if you plug in a TV or console. Check the port count before you buy.

Labels like AX3000 or BE10000 add all bands together. No single device gets that figure, and in practice the speed depends on distance and walls. A BE10000 label on the Deco 7 Pro does not mean 10 Gbps to your phone. Use the label to compare tiers, not to predict speed.

Some brands put parental controls, security and advanced features behind a subscription. Check what the free tier includes for the eero 6+ and Orbi. Firmware support length also matters, since a router sits on your network for years. A system with regular updates is safer than a cheaper one that is abandoned.

howWeEvaluated.title: Backhaul design
howWeEvaluated.description: We read how each system links its nodes. The Deco 7 Pro and Deco XE75 are tri-band, and the Deco X55 and eero 6+ are dual-band. We weighted tri-band and wired options, based on the spec sheet.

howWeEvaluated.title: Generation and ports
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared Wi-Fi 6, 6E and 7, and the Ethernet ports. The Deco 7 lists 2.5G ports, while the Deco X55 does not. These are editorial assessments from published specifications.

howWeEvaluated.title: Coverage realism
howWeEvaluated.description: We treated every square footage claim as a best case. The Orbi 770 at 8,000 and the eero 6+ at 4,500 show the range, and we adjusted for typical walls.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at app quality, firmware and subscriptions. Based on patterns in owner feedback, setup is easy on all six, and paid extras are the common complaint.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value tier
howWeEvaluated.description: We ordered systems on a one to eleven relative price scale. The Deco X55 at tier three and the Orbi 770 at tier ten define the spread.

cards.label: Wi-Fi 6E
cards.text: The Deco XE75 adds the 6 GHz band and tri-band backhaul at a lower tier, with gigabit ports.

cards.label: Wi-Fi 7
cards.text: The Deco 7, Deco 7 Pro and Orbi 770 add wider channels and 2.5G ports, but need Wi-Fi 7 devices to shine.

howToChoose.note: Choose 6E for value and tri-band now; choose Wi-Fi 7 if you want to keep the system for many years.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A system that handles many devices, a clean 2.4 GHz band and a stable app. Bandwidth matters less than reliable connections.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The NETGEAR Orbi 770 lists 100 devices, and the TP-Link Deco XE75 offers tri-band capacity at a lower tier.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your home is large, your plan is above one gigabit or you can wire nodes. The Deco 7 Pro and Orbi 770 suit that.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your home is mid-size on a gigabit plan. The Deco X55 or eero 6+ cover that at lower tiers.

maintenance.why: Updates fix security issues and stability. Most systems update automatically, but confirm in the app.
Nodes placed too far apart lose speed. Move it about halfway between the main node and the dead zone.
A restart clears stuck connections and memory. Do it when the network feels sluggish.
Dust traps heat, which shortens electronics life. Wipe vents with a dry cloth.
Paid features may renew automatically. Check whether you still use them.

faq.q: Do I need mesh or is a good router enough?
faq.a: A single good router is enough for a small home or apartment. Mesh helps when walls and floors block signal. If one router reaches every room, skip mesh.
Only if you have Wi-Fi 7 devices or want future proofing. Most homes still see little change over Wi-Fi 6. A Deco 7 is a reasonable step for long-term use.

faq.q: How many nodes do I need?
faq.a: A three-pack covers most large homes, and two nodes suit smaller ones. Count floors and thick walls. More nodes in a bad layout do not fix a bad placement.
Yes, if you can. Ethernet between nodes avoids the speed loss of a wireless hop. It also lets you upgrade the Wi-Fi standard later.

faq.q: Do speed labels like AX3000 mean real speed?
faq.a: No. They add all bands together. Your device speed depends on distance, walls and its own Wi-Fi support.

faq.q: Are mesh systems safe to leave running?
faq.a: They are designed for continuous use and draw on the order of 10 to 20 watts per node. Keep vents clear, apply firmware updates and use a surge protector.
